The melody side has one or more rows of buttons, each row giving one diatonic scale; the bass buttons are mostly in pairs, one giving the root of the chord and the other a major triad, occasionally a minor triad. It is popular in many countries, mainly in popular music, traditional folk music and their modern offshoots.
梅洛迪恩風琴屬自由簧氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號412.13: The melodeon is a free-reed aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 412.132. Each of the one or more rows of buttons on the melody side corresponds to a diatonic scale, and most use a single-action or bisonoric reed system: the same button gives two notes, one on the push and one on the pull of the bellows, the push notes mostly belonging to the tonic major triad and the pull notes filling out the diatonic scale. Each row covers usually about two full octaves, with a few extra notes above and below. The bass buttons are in pairs, giving the root of the chord and the major triad, sometimes the minor triad. Unlike unisonoric instruments such as the piano or the chromatic button accordion, the direction of the bellows is closely tied to pitch and to the harmony available; the harmonica and the bandoneon of the same family are also single-action. 梅洛迪恩風琴屬自由簧氣鳴樂器，其遠祖可追溯至西元前3000年中國與老撾的笙與 k: The melodeon is a free-reed aerophone whose distant ancestors go back to the sheng and the khene of China and Laos around 3000 BC; European travellers of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries brought back descriptions and pictures. In the early nineteenth century the free-reed principle met mechanised mass production, and instruments such as the accordion appeared. On 6 May 1829 Cyrill Demian took out a patent, the original design being mainly for chordal accompaniment. After that Louis Douce developed the single-note accordion in 1840 and Franz Walther built a chromatic button accordion in 1850; at the end of the nineteenth century Paolo Soprani mass-produced the bisonoric system, three-row keyboards appeared in the early twentieth century, and the German firm Hohner pressed for the standardisation of the two-row diatonic layout. In Britain and Australia the instrument is generally called a melodeon, while in Ireland the word mostly means the single-row instrument.
